articles.title: Duvaktig Fed men negativa börsterminer – fokus nu på ECB och mycket svenskdata
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Kommentarer åt det mjukare hållet från Fed-chefen Warsh efter beskedet om oförändrad ränta (mer nedan) gav något lägre korta räntor, en svagare USD och stöd åt aktiemarknaden. Både S&P 500 och Nasdaq stängde något högre (+0,3%). Efter stängning rapporterade techjättarna Microsoft och Alphabet; Microsoft klarade sig bra, medan Alphabet föll rejält, vilket har dragit ned både de amerikanska börsterminerna (Nasdaq −0,8%) och framför allt de techtunga asiatiska börserna (KOSPI −1,0% och Shenzhen −2,0%). Oljepriset har fallit under natten och handlas återigen kring 114 dollar per fat, då förhoppningar om fredssamtal tycks ha dämpat oron för ytterligare utbudsstörningar till följd av eskaleringen i Mellanöstern.
Oenigt Fed – lämnade styrräntan oförändrad i väntan på mer information.
 Fed lämnade igår kväll, som väntat, styrräntan oförändrad och inväntar ytterligare data. Två ledamöter, Cook och Hammack, reserverade sig till förmån för en räntehöjning på 25 punkter. Den största överraskningen var den något mjukare tonen från Fed-chefen Warsh under presskonferensen. Han framhöll att Fed har gjort framsteg genom att strama åt de finansiella förhållandena sedan september. Vi tolkar budskapet som förenligt med vår bedömning att Fed höjer räntan i december, men att utsikterna därefter är osäkra. Warsh mjukare ton har fått marknaden att minska sina förväntningar på Fed; nu prisas 82% sannolikhet för en höjning i december in jämfört med 94% innan räntebeskedet. Läs mer 
här
.
Storbritanniens budget lugnade marknaderna.
 Andy Bernhams första budget presenterades igår och den lyckades lugna marknaderna, främst genom att skjuta flera svåra beslut kring de offentliga utgifterna på framtiden (mer 
här
). Budgeten väntas inte påverka Bank of England nämnvärt inför nästa veckas räntemöte, där vi förväntar oss en höjning med 25 räntepunkter (mer på sidan 7 i gårdagens 
Ögat
). 
Dagens agenda
 domineras av räntebesked från ECB (mer nedan) och Amazons och Intels rapporter (efter USA börsens stängning). Den innehåller även en hel del viktiga svenska data, Feds favoritinflationsmått PCE samt den första uppskattningen av USA:s tillväxt under det tredje kvartalet (mer nedan). Missa inte heller att Japans centralbank kommer med sitt räntebesked redan kl. 04.00 på fredagsmorgonen. 
ECB väntas lämna räntan oförändrad idag, 
fokus blir på presskonferensen kl. 14:45. Energipriserna talar för uppåtrisker för inflationen, men utfallen har i stort följt ECB:s prognoser och några tydliga andrahandseffekter via löner syns ännu inte. Samtidigt pekar företagsenkäter på fortsatt förbättring i ekonomin även om konsumentförtroendet är svagt. Högre långräntor har dessutom stramat åt de finansiella förhållandena och minskat behovet av fler omedelbara räntehöjningar. Vi räknar fortsatt med två höjningar om 25 punkter, i december 2026 och mars 2027. Läs mer i vår ECB Preview 
här
.
Feds favoritinflationsmått PCE väntas ha stigit i linje med KPI.
 Kärn-KPI steg med 0,3 procent i september och vi räknar med en liknande uppgång för kärn-PCE. Höga flygbiljettpriser enligt PPI bidrar till uppåttryck, medan lägre priser på hälso- och sjukvård utgör en nedåtrisk. De månatliga prisökningarna är fortsatt högre än vad som är förenligt med inflationsmålet och kärn-PCE ligger betydligt högre än kärn-KPI även efter nedrevideringen. En högre inflationssiffra i dag skulle få marknaden att återigen prisa in större sannolikhet för en räntehöjning i december. 
I vår serie av Nordic Outlook Updates
 har idag turen kommit till de två stora ekonomierna 
Kina
 och 
Indien
. Fram till tisdag 10 november publicerar vi löpande våra prognoser och vår syn på den makroekonomiska utvecklingen i enskilda länder och regioner på vår 
Researchsida
.
Sverige
Mycket makrodata på agendan.
 BNP för tredje kvartalet, KI:s barometrar och detaljhandeln för september publiceras alla kl. 08.00. BNP-indikatorn har planat ut under de två första månaderna av tredje kvartalet efter ett starkt andrakvartal ; vi räknar med att BNP-tillväxten bromsar in till 2,9 procent från 3,3 procent föregående kvartal. I KI:s barometrar väntar vi oss en viss dämpning när högre energipriser och väntade räntehöjningar från Riksbanken tynger hushåll och företag. Prisplanerna lär samtidigt förbli höga, medan arbetsmarknadsindikatorerna blir viktiga att följa för tecken på avmattning. Vi räknar också med ytterligare en ökning i detaljhandeln i september, men en längre period med höga energipriser och stigande räntor utgör en tydlig nedåtrisk för våra optimistiska tillväxtprognoser.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - India
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts.    
Robust growth pushed our 2026 GDP forecast to 7.5 per cent, though momentum is expected to cool as investment peaks. Structural tailwinds support domestic demand, but rural consumption is expected to lag as El Niño hurts agriculture. Food prices will soon push inflation above 6 per cent, prompting the RBI to tighten further. Widening trade deficit, weak capital flows, and elevated oil prices pressure the rupee. This will prompt the RBI to favour more regulatory intervention to defend the USD/IND around 97.  
GDP growth continues to surprise to the upside, prompting another upward revision to our 2026 forecast to 7.5 per cent from 6.8 per cent. Near-term growth will likely ease in Q4 2026 as investment activity shows signs of topping out. Even so, industrial production remains resilient despite elevated energy prices. 
Strong structural and demographic tailwinds continue to support long-term domestic demand. Yet near-term cyclical risks are emerging. Strong output in consumer durables outpace non-durables, reflecting the surge in urban consumption. Even so, rural demand is faltering. Agricultural headwinds flagged in our August report have materialized, as indicated by the pullback in two-wheeler sales. 
Fiscal policy has absorbed the impact of the Iran war shock. Higher crude oil prices inflated subsidy costs, likely widening the government deficit to 4.6 percent of GDP against the budgeted 4.3 per cent target. Although bond yields have already climbed alongside inflation and global rates, persistent high oil prices present ongoing upside risks to domestic yields. 
Price pressures are rising, as expected. Headline inflation will likely breach the central bank’s 6 per cent upper threshold in the near term, driven by food’s 35 per cents weighting in the CPI basket. While energy subsidies cushioned against the impact of high crude oil prices, severe El Niño conditions have already started to drive up food costs. The severity and location of the drought will dictate 2027 crop yields and food inflation. 
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised policy rate in October, signalling “calibrated” tightening that limits expectations to a maximum of 2 further hikes. We expect one more rate increase to 5.75 per cent by end-2026. As rate differentials will offer little support, the central bank must deploy regulatory measures to defend the rupee. 
Balance of payments pressures will continue to weigh on the rupee. A widening trade deficit, exacerbated by limited export exposure to global AI infrastructure spending, and contracting foreign equity flows reinforce currency weakness. Following volatile movements in FX reserves in 2026, the RBI introduced regulatory friction in October to stem rupee depreciation while conserving FX reserves. Although these tools should keep the USD/INR below 97 in the near term, elevated oil prices, a robust dollar, and weak capital flows will cap any sustained currency recovery .

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - China
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts.  
China’s growth target of 4.5-5.0 percent is secure. Strong exports and a recovery in oil refinery activity offset weak domestic demand and a persistently contracting property sector. The trade surplus is on track to top USD 1.2 trillion, though EU trade friction poses risks for 2027. Muted consumer inflation allows for a supportive monetary policy. Rising foreign currency deposits support a steady appreciation of the yuan toward 6.60 against the greenback. 
China’s growth target of 4.5-5.0 per cent for 2026 appears secure. Sufficient acceleration in September activity eased the pressure on policymakers to dial up stimulus. Robust exports and a rebound in crude oil refining lifted Q3 GDP growth to 4.5 percent. With growth running at 4.6 percent year-to-date, the economy is on track to hit the target even if growth moderates in Q4. 
Domestic demand continues to weigh on growth, constrained by weak consumer confidence and a stagnant labour market. Investment has contracted, exacerbated by cautious government stimuli. A near-term boost to public spending is expected. Beijing has allowed provincial governments to tap CNY 550 billion (USD 82 billion) in unused bond quotas from previous years. Yet, the appetite for further stimulus hinges entirely on whether the economic performance hits the official growth target. 
The worst of the shock from the war with Iran appears to have passed. Refinery capacity utilization has improved, sitting less than 8 per cent below its pre-war average by mid-October. Although crude oil imports have climbed steadily since July, year-to-date volumes remain 15 percent lower than in the same period in 2025. This points to greater reliance on domestic inventories. Recent directives from Beijing urging energy firms to boost production and build up reserves suggest that imports will continue to rise in the coming quarters. 
Exports remain the primary engine of growth, fueled by sustained global demand for AI infrastructure that shows no signs of abating. Strong shipments to key markets put the full year trade surplus on track to eclipse the record USD 1.2 trillion set in 2025.
Trade frictions with the EU looms. With the surplus with the EU set to surpass USD 350 billion in 2026, Brussels is pushing back. Despite a recent agreement capping hybrid car exports, the block is reportedly preparing new curbs on imports of chemicals, furniture and machinery. These measures could take effect as early as 2027. 
Despite a rise in factory-gate prices, passthrough to consumer inflation remains muted. Weak inflationary pressures leave the central bank room to maintain a supportive stance. While the interest rate gap with the US broadens, the central bank continues to steadily strengthen the yuan. The yuan is further supported by the huge trade surpluses that have left domestic banks flushing with foreign currency deposits. The year-end USD/CNY forecast stands unchanged at 6.60 with further appreciation expected in 2027.

articles.title: Split Fed left rates unchanged, waiting for more information
articles.heading: Fed decision
articles.fulltext:
The Fed, as expected, left its policy rate unchanged, awaiting more data. Also, as expected, the Fed was split, as two members – Cook and Hammack – dissented in favour of a 25 bp hike. The main surprise was instead the somewhat softer language by Fed Chair Warsh in the press conference, where he said that the Fed had made progress by tightening financial conditions since September. We see the message as supportive of our expectations that the Fed will deliver another rate increase in December but that the pace thereafter is uncertain. 
Key points
Fed voted 10-2 for unchanged rate at 3.75-4.00%
Cook and Hammack wanted to raise rates
Waiting for information in line with message from Williams, Jefferson and Waller
Fed has become more optimistic about growth
Warsh sees progress since September
Balance sheet will be discussed in Q1
Fewer policy meetings, with some devoted to strategy talks instead
Dovish market reactions
We continue to expect one more hike in December
Waiting for more information in line with the signals from key FOMC members 
The Fed, as expected, left its policy rate unchanged within the range of 3.75-4.00%. According to the statement “the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate
to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.” This is very much in line with the reasoning of key policy members (Williams, Jefferson and Waller) ahead of the meeting, where they said there was no urgency in tightening policy again but that the Fed could give itself time to gather more information. It is also fully in line with the median forecast in the September projections, which indicated one more rate increase until year-end, rather than successive rate increases at the remaining two meetings in October and December.
The Fed remains split about the need for tighter policy
Two members – Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack – voted for raising rates by 25 bp. We thought the dissent would come from Hammack and Logan, though it is worth noting that Logan has also highlighted the tightening effect of rising yields. In July, Hammack, Logan and Kashkari dissented; now we have a fourth member voting for a hike. This highlights how diverse views are within the Fed, where some members according to the September minutes saw rate increases as necessary, given their inflation outlook, but where many viewed them rather as taking out insurance. Notably, Cook has again come under attack from the White House, after the earlier attempt to oust her from the Fed was stopped by the Supreme Court. Her decision to vote for a hike is unlikely to make President Trump feel more warmly about her. 
The Fed sees stronger growth
The policy statement was, like earlier, short, with only small changes apart from the sentence on getting more information. There was a small shift in the description of the economy, where economic activity was described as expanding at a “strong”, rather than “solid” pace, showing an upgrade in the Fed’s view of the economy. This was also the message from Chair Warsh’s introductory statement, where he said the economy had strengthened (in September he said it appeared to be strengthening) and where he in general conveyed a positive view of the economy, including signs that investments seem to be broadening into other areas outside high-tech. 
Warsh sees “progress” since September
The Fed – and Warsh – at the same time, seem to have become slightly more optimistic about its ability to get inflation back to target. Thus, according to the statement, the Fed says it is looking at a “timely”, rather than as in September “timelier” return of inflation to the inflation target. This message was also reflected in the introductory statement at the press conference, where Warsh highlighted a tightening of financial and credit conditions since September. However, he also said he is “unwilling and unable to call financial conditions tight”, which suggests that Warsh thinks that the Fed has more work to do. In the Q&A, Warsh said he was encouraged by the progress the Fed had made in a short period of time and specifically pointed to the fact that inflation compensation in for instance swaps and inflation expectations had moved the right way, considering the movements in energy prices. 
More dovish Warsh again
We think one should be careful in drawing conclusions from the communication at the meeting, given Warsh insistence on not giving forward guidance. We also think that given the comments from Williams, Jefferson and Waller it would not have been possible to unite the Fed behind another rate increase already in October, and that Warsh is striving for unanimous decisions when hiking rates. But, if anything, the language of Warsh was more dovish than at Jackson Hole or after the September meeting. Warsh continued to stress that inflation is too high and pointed to rising energy prices and the need for the Fed to make sure that relative price changes in some sectors (i.e. rising prices on not only energy but also IT-related goods) do not broaden out across the economy. But he avoided a repeat of many of his previous hawkish statements. 
He did not discuss recent inflation developments, where he has earlier said that he did not see “meaningful” signs of progress.
 We see this as in line with another rate increase in December but not necessarily a series of rate increases. 
“Information rich” period ahead
Going forward, Warsh highlighted the “information rich” period ahead, including geopolitical developments, movements in energy prices and technology changes, which will inform the Fed’s next step. 
Balance sheet will be discussed in Q1
When it comes to the Fed’s balance sheet, there were no changes in the statement. The Fed continues its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. On a direct question Warsh said the Fed will await the recommendations from the task force and that these will feed into the Fed’s considerations in the first quarter next year. Warsh has earlier called for the Fed to resume shrinking the balance sheet, but any changes will thus have to wait until next year, and they will only be made after “serious consideration” of the recommendations of the task force. 
Fewer policy meetings, with some devoted to strategy talks instead 
Apart from the policy decision, Warsh also announced a change in the Fed’s meeting schedule. Starting in fall 2027, the Fed will devote one of its eight meetings to a discussion of monetary policy strategy and will not decide about rates or issue a policy statement at this meeting. In 2028, two of the eight meetings will be devoted to strategy and six to policy decisions. 
Dovish market reactions
Markets had an initial hawkish reaction to the statement but made a dovish interpretation of Warsh’s comments. Yields increased a couple of bp after the statement but declined thereafter, with 2-year yields down almost 10 bp at the most and 5-year by 5 bp compared to before the announcement. The tech-heavy Nasdaq turned higher again. Markets continue to price a high probability for a December hike (21 bp) and almost two full hikes by March, but pricing further out has become a tad less aggressive with markets anticipating more than 2 ½ increases by year-end 2027, but not fully three hikes. Longer-dated yields were little changed, resulting in a renewed steepening of the curve.
We continue to expect one more hike in December
We stick to our forecast for another rate increase at the December meeting, but that the Fed will leave rates unchanged thereafter before returning to rate cuts again by late 2027. We see both upside risks, related to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the risk that persistently elevated energy prices spread into other prices, and downside risks, from rising real yields and new bouts of market unrest

articles.title: A Budget "in hock" to the bond market
articles.heading: United Kingdom
articles.fulltext:
The Budget was broadly in line with our expectations, 
providing targeted support to households and businesses while laying the groundwork for more ambitious longer-term reforms and pushing larger spending decisions into the future, as outlined in our Budget primer.
The main measures include a £100 council tax rebate for lower- and middle-income households, an extension of the energy VAT relief, as well as lower import tariffs on food and higher minimum wages. For companies, electricity bills were reduced by 25% for roughly 10,000 manufacturers, and tax reliefs for high-street businesses. The spending commitments are partly financed by higher taxes on banks, gambling and other minor areas, as well as increased borrowing in the near term. Overall, the fiscal package (£11.6bn) is considerably smaller than previous Budgets under Rachel Reeves, but it contains its fair share of reforms. With 98 reforms, it includes more than Reeves' "smorgasbord" Budget, and double compared to the average
The Budget focuses on stimulating private investment through innovation and greater regional devolution. 
A central theme is the additional £20.4bn in financing capacity for Public Financial Institutions (PuFIns). As mentioned, these investments have a limited impact on the PSNFL debt measure underpinning the fiscal rule but still require additional gilt issuance. Of this, £15bn is targeted towards infrastructure and industrial revival, while £5bn is targeted towards innovation and start-ups. Additional support will be given to start-ups and innovation through easier access to R&D funding and less regulatory hurdles.
The government also presented a roadmap for fiscal devolution, with regional authorities gradually retaining more tax revenues, and argued that this would lead to higher growth. However, greater regional autonomy does not automatically generate growth. As we highlighted in our piece on Manchesterism, devolution in Scotland and Wales has not eliminated their growth and productivity gaps. Manchester's experience has been more positive, but the aggregate economic benefits remain uncertain.
The main surprise was the OBR's downgrade to its 2027 GDP growth forecast, from 1.6% to 1.0%.
 The downgrade for 2027 is primarily driven by higher energy prices and interest rates reducing real incomes and household consumption, while higher borrowing costs weigh on investment and demand. Growth for 2026 was revised by 0.1 percentage points, while the outlook for 2028 remained unchanged. Healey's comment that the government would prove the OBR's growth forecasts wrong is a potential warning sign of excessive faith in its own policies.
CPI inflation in 2027 has been revised up from around 2% to 3.4%. The OBR expects both direct effects from higher household energy prices and indirect effects as higher production and transportation costs feed through to other goods and services, including food. Some second-round effects through wage growth are also expected, although less than in 2022, given a significantly looser labour market. Inflation is expected to return to target in 2028, but real earnings are forecast to stagnate in both 2027 and 2028.
Public finances have deteriorated, mainly because of higher debt interest costs. 
The OBR has revised borrowing in 2026/27 up by £17.7bn to £133.2bn (4.2% of GDP), with a further £15.5bn upward revision for 2027/28. The 2026/27 increase consists of £11.4bn from a weaker underlying fiscal forecast and £6.3bn from government policy decisions. Higher interest rates and inflation-linked debt costs increase expenditure, although stronger nominal incomes and corporate profits also generate additional tax revenues, partly offsetting the deterioration.
The government's fiscal rules are still met, with £15bn of headroom against the stability rule, down from £23.6bn in March. However, the OBR estimates only a 56% probability of meeting the rule, compared with 59% at the November 2025 Budget. The probability of meeting the investment rule has increased slightly from 52% to 54%.
The main concern is that spending is front-loaded while fiscal tightening is postponed, as warned in our primer. Much of the later improvement relies on higher tax receipts and restraint in departmental spending, including reductions that have yet to be fully specified. This leaves the government vulnerable if growth disappoints or future spending pressures increase. With debt interest costs projected to reach £160bn by 2031/32, the scope for further fiscal surprises is limited. 
The important change for the gilt market is the issuance profile. 
The DMO's financing requirement rises by £7.4bn from April to £258.6bn. This is financed through an additional £4.4bn of gilt issuance, bringing total planned gilt sales to £250.6bn. Compared with the April remit, planned short-dated conventional issuance increases by £12.6bn to £107.6bn and medium-dated issuance by £13.3bn to £89.3bn. This is financed partly by reducing the previously unallocated issuance programme by £14.9bn and cutting long-dated issuance by £6.9bn to just £15.5bn. Long-dated conventional gilts now account for only 6.2% of planned issuance, compared with 9.1% in April. This continues the shift towards shorter maturities highlighted in our earlier research and will make government finances more sensitive to changes in interest rates.
This continues the shift towards shorter maturities highlighted in our analysis. Lower long-dated supply should provide relative support to the 20–30-year sector, while increased short- and medium-dated issuance could put some pressure on these maturities. However, moving issuance towards shorter maturities increases future refinancing requirements and the sensitivity of government finances to interest-rate changes.
The initial market reaction has been relatively muted. 
Gilt yields declined ahead of and immediately after the Budget before partly reversing, leaving the 2-year yield broadly unchanged and the 10-year yield down a few basis points. The issuance profile, with reduced supply of long-dated gilts and increased short-dated issuance, supported a flattening of the gilt curve. Sterling was little changed over the day, although it appreciated slightly against the dollar and the euro in the aftermath of the Budget. Equities were broadly unchanged, with banks rallying in the morning on news of a smaller-than-anticipated bank tax increase.
Ultimately, the government has bought itself some breathing space without resolving its longer-term fiscal challenges. The more difficult test will come when its growth ambitions must be translated into stronger economic performance and fully financed spending plans.

articles.title: RBNZ Pauses Hikes, Grounding the Kiwi
articles.heading: Central Bank Insights
articles.fulltext:
Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) surprised the market by keeping the policy rate at 2.75%. Yet, the inflation target demands a return to tightening by December. A reluctant RBNZ forces a re-assessment of our NZD/USD yearend target of 0.58. Current market pricing for RBNZ is overstretched relative to what the fundamentals can bear. With the RBA ready to fly and the RBNZ clipping its own wings, expectations of rate convergence will fade. We expect AUD/NZD to find fresh buyers on any dip around 1.248. 
Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) surprised the market by keeping the policy rate steady at 2.75%. 
In a 4-3 vote split, the Monetary Policy Committee left the market wrong-footed as market consensus virtually guaranteed a 25bps hike. Governor Breman and three fellow committee members preferred to pause and assess the lagged impact of earlier back-to-back rate increases since July. Since New Zealand pioneered formal inflation targeting in 1990, price stability has been the central bank’s North Star. The current remit specifies an inflation target range of 1-3% (Chart 1). 
Chart 1: RBNZ surprises with unchanged policy rate despite elevated inflation
Source: CEIC, SEB
RBNZ may be taking a tactical breather, but the inflation target demands a return to tightening by December. 
 The undeniable surge in tradables inflation is compounded by sticky non-tradables prices running above the 3% threshold. Broadening price pressures, sticky inflation expectations and elevated business pricing intentions leave little margin for comfort (Chart 2). Persistent global energy market disruptions mean that enterprises can no longer delay passing on higher input costs to consumers. Overall, there is little room for RBNZ to prolong the pause, in our view. 
Chart 2: Inflation expectations and pricing intentions point to price pressures
Source: CEIC, SEB
Although RBNZ is signalling tighter policy looms in the near term, it has attached a heavy leash to its hawkishness. 
During the press conference, Governor Breman has reiterated that rate hikes are “conditional” on the data. While every committee member concurs that higher rates loom, the majority felt constrained by the mixed growth outlook. Although business surveys point to continued growth, caution reigned supreme today. Household consumption is weak and saving rates are well above historic norms. 
A reluctant RBNZ forces a re-assessment of our NZD/USD yearend target of 0.58. 
The Kiwi took a beating after traders found themselves on the wrong side of the trade. The pair plunged more than 1% to a low of 0.5590 immediately after the announcement. Historically, the RBNZ’s single-minded focus on inflation led markets to price in an aggressive tightening path. We reiterate our view that the central bank has space to hike 50bps through Q1 2027. Conversely, market is still pricing in over 100 bps in hikes over the next 12 months even after the unchanged policy stance today. Yet, the RBNZ’s hesitation today proves that market has sprinted ahead of economic reality. Higher rates may be looming. Yet, Governor Breman has already indicated that conditions are good for inflation to slow down in 2027. Overall, 
current market pricing for RBNZ is overstretched relative to what the fundamentals can bear.
The RBNZ’s hesitation removed a near term speed limit to AUD/NZD. 
While the cross is still trading above market implied policy rate differential (Chart 3). Today’s pause forces a reality check. A stark contrast in policy bias between the Antipodean central banks has been highlighted. RBA stands ready to act after the hotter-than-expected Q3 CPI print prompted RBA Governor Bullock to question if policy is tight enough. With the RBA ready to fly and the RBNZ clipping its own wings, expectations of rate convergence will fade. 
We expect AUD/NZD to find fresh buyers on any dip around 1.248.  
Chart 3: Hopes of rate convergence will fade, lifting the cap on AUD/NZD
Source: Bloomberg, SEB

articles.title: Retail sales continue its sideways trend
articles.heading: Norwegian retail sales
articles.fulltext:
Retail sales ex. autos declined 0.4% m/m in September, leaving Q3 unchanged from the previous quarter. The details were mixed: retail sales from food stores weighed on the monthly figures while clothing, furniture and electrical appliances provided support. Goods consumption likely rose in Q3, mainly reflecting a surge within private car registrations. Looking ahead, weak consumer confidence suggests continued caution, although rising purchasing power should provide some support. We expect household consumption to strengthen as households increasingly shift from savings to spending, making consumption an increasingly important driver of growth. 
Details
Retail sales ex. autos: 
Retail sales ex. autos fell 0.4% m/m in September, following a 0.6% m/m increase in August. Quarterly growth thus ended flat compared to the previous quarter suggesting that momentum remains subdued. Sub sectors deviated somewhat; the largest basket of retail sales in non-specialised stores (predominantly food etc.) dropped substantially (-2.1% m/m) and were the main drag on the headline figures. This was partly offset by an increase in household equipment, including furniture and electrical appliances (0.1% m/m) and retail other goods, including clothes and footwear (0.8% m/m). The year-on-year decline narrowed to 1.0% y/y. Sales of automotive fuel and information and communication equipment remained particularly weak, down 15.9% and 4.6% y/y, respectively. The first is likely related to the subsidies put down by the government following higher energy prices which was in effect until September 2026. The effect is thus temporary and will likely rebound in the coming month. Weak consumer confidence in Q3 points to continued caution among households, while a rising saving ratio poses a downside risk to consumption growth this year. Strong real wage growth and still-low unemployment should provide some support.
Publication of the monthly household goods consumption indicator, which feeds into the national accounts, has been postponed indefinitely owing to a major benchmark revision. Retail sales and car registration data nevertheless provide some indications of developments in goods consumption.
These indicators also painted a mixed picture in September. Consumption of food, beverages and tobacco declined 1.9% m/m while other goods consumption edged up 0.1% m/m. Meanwhile, private car registrations surged 11.4% m/m taking year-on-year growth to 36.7%. Taken together, the available indicators point to an increase in goods consumption in September, mainly driven by private car registrations. 
Implications Norges Bank:
 Household consumption accounts for a substantial share of mainland GDP. Growth has been weaker than Norges Bank expected so far this year, prompting the Bank to lower its forecast for household consumption in 2026 to 0.8%.
A weak start to the year due to front-loading of purchases of electrical vehicles in 2025 explains parts of this weakness. The timing of Easter has also complicated the interpretation of seasonally adjusted developments in Q2. Weak consumer confidence and a rising savings ratio argues for cautious household spending for the remainder of the year. On the other hand, contacts from the Regional Network report resilient household demand. We expect rising purchasing power to support a recovery in consumption towards year-end, followed by stronger growth in 2027. Norges Bank forecasts household consumption growth of 2.6% next year. 
Retail sales data remain volatile, but overall developments are still consistent with softer demand.

articles.title: Neutral SEK portfolio rebalancing requirements in October
articles.heading: Rebalancing flows
articles.fulltext:
Our model estimates that typical Swedish portfolio managers will have broadly neutral SEK requirements in their monthly currency rebalancing this October. The most pronounced flows are buying JPY and selling USD, although the estimated rebalancing needs in these currencies are relatively modest. The stylised portfolio gained 0.4% in October, bringing its year-to-date return to 4.4%.
Neutral SEK requirements
This October, rebalancing implies SEK purchases of 0.04% of the portfolio. The largest need, however, is to buy JPY (+0.2%) and sell USD (-0.2%).
Neutral requirements in SEK. Most pronounced need to buy JPY and sell USD
Historical outcomes of SEK rebalancing needs
Source: SEB
Portfolio implications 
Currency hedge:
 The stylised portfolio used in our analysis gained 0.4% in October, which implies only a very small need to rebalance the hedge ratios (corresponding to -0.03% of the portfolio).
Bonds & Equity
: 
Relative monthly performance points to a very small need to buy Swedish equities (corresponding to 0.03% of the portfolio) and a minimal need to buy Swedish bonds. Together, the allocation rebalancing implies net SEK purchases of 0.01% of the portfolio.
Market developments October
All in all:
 Combining the hedge and allocation rebalancing needs results in total SEK purchases of 0.04% of the portfolio in October.

articles.title: Fed on hold, raises rates later this year
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
US equity markets closed higher yesterday; the S&P 500 rose by 0.6% and the more tech-heavy Nasdaq by 1.2%. Overnight, Asian markets are mixed but mostly higher on renewed optimism about technology stocks. Japan’s Nikkei has gained just over 1%, but South Korea is the strongest performer (up more than 6%), with technology stocks leading the gains after SK Hynix, among others, reported strong results and promised substantial dividends. Ahead of the Fed’s decision and key earnings reports, including Microsoft and Alphabet today, futures point to a slightly lower in Europe and slightly higher in the US ahead of todays trading. Brazil’s Bolsonaro has arrived in the US after losing the election in Brazil. Oil prices have risen slightly overnight following reports that the US has told countries around the Persian Gulf to prepare for a short but intense attack after the US midterm elections. 
Central banks take centre stage in today’s calendar.
 Today’s calendar has a strong central bank focus, with decisions from the Fed and the Bank of Canada (more below). German consumer confidence (GfK) may offer some clues about the German economy and the progress of the economic recovery. 
A split election in Israel.
 Support appears roughly evenly split between Netanyahu’s governing coalition and the opposition bloc, while the number of parliamentary seats held by Arab parties (outside both blocs) is increasing; forming a government will be difficult in Israel too. 
Fed: Anything other than unchanged rates would be a major surprise – a rate hike is coming in December.
 Following more dovish comments from some Fed officials and somewhat more nervous equity markets recently, markets are pricing in a probability of more than 90 per cent that rates will remain unchanged. The outlook is uncertain, with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, the strength of the US economy and developments in financial conditions all important factors. We maintain our assessment that the Fed will raise rates once more in December, followed by rate cuts towards the end of 2027 and during the first half of 2028. Read Elisabet Kopelman’s Fed Preview 
here
. 
New Zealand holds steady; Canada is expected to raise rates.
 Overnight, New Zealand’s central bank unexpectedly left rates unchanged in a split decision, citing global uncertainty weighing on the economy; the currency fell following the announcement. The Bank of Canada is expected to raise rates from 2.25% to 2.50% as inflation rises and GDP grows at a healthy pace. 
UK budget postpones the difficult decisions. 
Prime Minister Burnham has ambitious plans to kick-start the economy, but policy is constrained by already high taxes and large deficits. Given high interest rates and the focus on government finances, the budget proposal being presented today will be of interest to both political observers and markets. It is likely to be a cautious budget focused on households and small businesses, in the hope of avoiding market jitters and of gaining more room to fund further reforms if growth picks up and energy prices and interest rates fall. Read more 
here
. 
A new Nordic Outlook is on the way!
 Today’s analysis of 
Japan
marks the launch of the Nordic Outlook Update. Between now and Tuesday, 10 November, we will publish our forecasts and views on macroeconomic developments in individual countries and regions on our 
Research page
. On 10 November, we will publish our overall global outlook, including all the usual, eagerly awaited forecast tables.
Nordic key stories
Norwegian retail sales.
 Retail sales ex. autos rebounded in August, rising 0.6% m/m 
after the slump in previous month. Household consumption was week during H1, weighing on our full year estimate. Consumer confidence has recovered but continue to indicate cautions households. We expect higher purchasing power to underpin consumption ahead, with momentum improving into 2027.
Today’s Swedish calendar is relatively thin
, but tomorrow will bring more releases, with the National Institute of Economic Research’s Economic Tendency Survey and growth data. The krona strengthened slightly against the euro yesterday and has been relatively stable against both the euro and the dollar overnight.

articles.title: Fed avvaktar men höjer senare i år
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
USA-börserna stängde på plus igår; S&P500 steg med 0,6% och mer tekniktunga Nasdaq med 1,2%. Under natten är utvecklingen i Asien blandad men mest upp på förnyad tech-optimism. Japanska Nikkei har stigit med drygt 1% men bäst går det i Sydkorea (upp över 6%) där teknikaktier driver utvecklingen efter att bl a SK Hynix levererat en stark rapport och utlovat höga utdelningar. I väntan på Fed-besked och viktiga bolagsrapporter, idag från bl a Microsoft och Alphabet, pekar terminer svagt ner i Europa och svagt upp i USA inför dagens handel. Brasiliens Bolsonaro har landat i USA efter att ha förlorat valet i Brasilien. Oljepriser har stigit något över natten efter rapportering om att USA sagt åt länderna kring Persiska viken att förbereda sig på ett kort men intensivt anfall efter USA:s mellanårsval. 
Centralbanksfokus i dagens kalender.
 Dagens statistik har stort centralbanksfokus med besked från Fed och Kanada (mer nedan). Tyskt konsumentförtroende (GfK) kan ge lite ledtrådar kring tyska ekonomin och hur det går med tillväxtåterhämtningen. 
Splittrat val i Israel. 
Stödet ser ut att bli ungefär lika stort för Netanyahus regerande koalition och oppositionens block samtidigt som antalet parlamentsledamöter för arabiska partier (utanför båda blocken) ökar; en svår regeringsbildning även för Israel. 
Fed: Annat än en oförändrad ränta skulle vara en stor överraskning – räntehöjning kommer i december.
 Efter mjukare kommentarer från vissa Fed-ledamöter och lite mer nervösa börser den senaste tiden prissätter marknaden en sannolikhet på över 90 procent för ett oförändrat räntebesked. Utsikterna är osäkra och viktigt är den pågående konflikten i Mellanöstern, styrkan i den amerikanska ekonomin och utvecklingen av de finansiella förhållandena. Vi håller fast vid vår bedömning att Fed höjer räntan ytterligare en gång i december, följt av räntesänkningar mot slutet av 2027 och under första halvåret 2028. Läs Elisabet Kopelmans Fed Preview 
här
. 
Oförändrat från Nya Zeeland, Kanada väntas höja.
 Under natten lämnade Nya Zeelands centralbank, i ett splittrat besked, oväntat räntan oförändrad med hänvisning till att global osäkerhet tynger ekonomin; valutan föll på beskedet. Kanadas centralbank väntas höja från 2,25 till 2,50% när inflationen stiger och BNP ökar i god takt. 
Brittisk budget skjuter på de svåra besluten.
 Premiärminister Burnham har ambitiösa planer för att få igång ekonomin men politiken är bakbunden av redan höga skatter och stora underskott. Budgetförslaget som presenteras idag är med tanke på höga räntor och offentligfinansiellt fokus intressant för både politiskt intresserade och marknader. Troligen blir det en försiktig budget med fokus på hushåll och småföretag med förhoppning om att inte göra marknaden nervös och att utrymmet för att finansiera ytterligare reformer kommer att öka om tillväxt tar fart och energipriser och räntor faller. Läs mer 
här
.

 Vi går igenom förutsättningarna inför mellanårsvalet i USA den 3 november. Huvudscenariot är en demokratisk seger i båda kongressens kamrar, men utgången i senaten är fortfarande osäker. här

articles.title: Vad ändras med en demokratisk storseger?
articles.heading: Ögat
articles.fulltext:
Mellanårsvalet i USA står för dörren. En demokratisk seger i båda kongressens kamrar är huvudscenariot, men utgången i senaten är fortfarande osäker. En seger i representanthuset räcker för att blockera republikanernas finanspolitiska agenda, men president Trump behåller i båda fallen makten över utrikes-, immigrations- och handelspolitiken. 
Riksbanken höjer trots lägre inflation
Det mesta talar för att Riksbanken höjer styrräntan till 2 procent den 4 november. Direktionen har varit tydlig i sin kommunikation och trots att inflationen har blivit lägre än väntat tror vi på en höjning. Vi räknar också med att Riksbanken håller fast vid sin tidigare prognos med ytterligare höjningar nästa år. 
Globala centralbanksbeskeden duggar tätt
Vi befinner oss i en intensiv centralbanksperiod där i stort sett alla de centralbanker vi följer kommer att ge besked om räntan. Vi räknar med en höjning från Riksbanken, Bank of England, Bank of Canada och Reserve Bank of Australia, medan övriga förväntas lämna sina styrräntor oförändrade. 
Stigande varupriser i euroområdet beror inte på krigen
Varupriserna i euroområdet har stigit gradvis i år och inflationstakten ligger tydligt över det historiska genomsnittet. Men medan ECB:s fokus legat på indirekta effekter av högre energipriser, verkar uppgången hittills bero på ett skifte i ökningstakten för elektronikvaror. 
JPY och SEK kan gynnas av potentiellt marknadsskifte
Valutamarknadens fokus på högräntevalutor, vilket bland annat gett stöd åt dollarn, ser alltmer ut att gå mot ett skifte. Positioneringen är ansträngd och lägre energipriser och fallande räntor skulle ge stöd till lågräntevalutor som japanska yenen och den svenska kronan.

articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Japan
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts.
Policymakers are walking a tightrope as bond yields trade at multi-decade highs and the yen remains undervalued. The government must ease market concerns about public debt dynamics. Meanwhile, the Bank of Japan intends to normalise monetary policy as underlying inflation is close to the 2 per cent target. Japan’s economy has proven resilient, with domestic demand supported by high wage growth, fiscal stimulus, AI-demand supporting exports and a solid investment cycle. Growth is constrained by global risks and uncertainty over energy supply.
Japan’s government debt in relation to GDP, which is exceptionally high by international standards, will continue to decline in the coming years as nominal growth strengthens. Moreover, the debt is financed by domestic savings and central bank holdings, making it less dependent on foreign financing. However, debt dynamics are a bit worrisome. The duration of the public debt is around 9 years. When borrowing costs rise, and remain above long-term potential growth, domestic investors may demand compensation for increasing credit risks. 
The Takaichi government’s focus on expansionary economic policy (including a supportive monetary policy) – and signs that Japan has permanently left deflation behind – is testing markets. Risks to growth remain skewed to the downside over the forecast horizon. 
Domestic investment to support growth has long been insufficient. To raise potential growth, Japan is promoting investment in strategic sectors through close cooperation between the public and private sectors. High corporate profits, together with expectations of stronger productivity growth, should continue to support the domestic investment cycle.
To reduce the burden on low- and middle-income workers, the government will introduce benefits tailored to income levels on a full scale from FY2029. Japan will implement a two-year VAT reduction on food and beverages (from 8 to 2 per cent, starting in April 2027). Tokyo says that these measures will be financed without relying on deficit-financing bonds. Japanese policymakers are walking a tightrope as bond yields trade at multi-decade highs.
Nominal and real interest rates are expected to remain well below those in, for example, the US. Although rates remain low, they are higher than before, creating some headwinds for economic growth. The real policy rate will remain negative throughout the forecast period. 
Still, the yen is expected to receive support from (1) narrowing policy rate differentials with the US and the euro area, and (2) domestic financial investors who now find Japanese bond yields more attractive (hence limiting Japan’s export of capital to other countries). Over the forecast horizon, the current account surplus is expected to amount to USD 585bn.

articles.title: NOK 2bn in NST481 and NST490
articles.heading: NGB Spotlight
articles.fulltext:
On Wednesday Oct 28th, Norges Bank will hold a multiple tap auction where a total of NOK 2bn will be issued, split between the NST481 (1.75%, 09/2029) and the NST490 (4.125%, 06/2036) bonds. NST481 currently trades with a yield of 4.77%, implying a maturity-matched spread vs. Germany of 173bps and an ASW spread of -31.5bps. NST490 trades with a yield of 4.46%, with corresponding spread levels at 110bps and -12.25bps. The auction closes at 11.00 CET, and results will be available on Norges Bank’s website at 11.05 CET. 
Details
On Wednesday, Norges Bank will auction a total of NOK 2bn split between NST481 (09/2029) and the NST490 (06/2036) bonds. The longer tenor has been included in 11 auctions so far this year, as Norges Bank is aiming to build liquidity in the new 10y bond. The bond was also included in last week’s tap auction, where performance continued to be strong. So far this year, the bond has received an average bid-to-cover of 3.41 with an allotment share of 59%. The corresponding numbers for the 5 auctions in NST481 are 3.74 and 47%. We are not surprised that Norges Bank chooses to issue these bonds in the upcoming auction, and with the total volume capped at NOK 2bn we expect the auction to run smoothly.
Global bond markets have experienced significant volatility over the past month, with yields spiking sharply in early October before partially retracing. The 10Y US Treasury yield peaked at approximately 5.31% on Oct 5th before retracing and currently trading at ~5.00 %, while the 10Y Bund peaked near 3.49% and has since pulled back to 3.35%. NSTs have followed the global move: the 10Y NST yield reached a high of ~4.70% in early October and has since corrected to 4.46%, helping to stabilize spreads vs. Germany. NST ASW spreads continue to move largely sideways with lurking sellers in the mid-segment of the curve. Meanwhile, outright levels continue to attract demand from internationals. 
Expectations for Norges Bank have eased somewhat compared to last week with the market now discounting a 50/50 chance for another rate hike in December 2026 and still pricing in a full hike by March 2027. We reiterate our forecast that the hiking cycle has likely peaked, with policy easing not expected to begin before late 2027. Our inflation forecast is higher than Norges Bank’s near-term trajectory, but we predict slightly lower core inflation in 2027. 
Supply update: Following this auction, Norges Bank has issued a total of NOK 101bn YTD, while the annual borrowing interval is set at NOK 100-110bn (107-110bn in the Q4 guidance). We expect Norges Bank to issue the maximum amount, implying NOK 3bn in one of the 4 remaining auctions and NOK 2bn for the remaining auctions.
Supply 2027:
 The government’s budget proposal for 2027 showed an underlying borrowing requirement of NOK 93.6bn vs. 95.7bn in 2026. After years of under-borrowing, Norges Bank’s supply estimate has exceeded the underlying borrowing requirement over the past two years, with the aim of building up the cash reserves. We expect this to be the case also in 2027, implying a minimum of NOK 110bn in gross supply. The government’s borrowing mandate in long-term debt is increased by NOK 50bn to NOK 200bn, to provide greater flexibility and allowing for a potential increase in its own holdings. Risks to our supply estimate are thus skewed to the upside. Details will be provided in Norges Bank’s Strategy and borrowing programme due in December.
